content: Recent immigrants and refugees represent a significant proportion of malaria cases in the United States, accounting for nearly 10% of imported malaria cases among individuals with known resident status in 2006. This report details three cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria and two cases of Plasmodium ovale malaria that occurred between June 27 and October 15, 2007, in King County, Washington. These infections were diagnosed in Burundian refugees who had recently arrived in the United States from two refugee camps in Tanzania. The infections highlight the importance of vigilance for malaria among healthcare providers caring for recently arrived refugees, even those who have received prior treatment for the disease. Rising resistance to traditional malaria treatments, such as chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, led the CDC to recommend presumptive treatment with artemether-lumefantrine for sub-Saharan African refugees before their departure to the United States. However, implementation of this recommendation was delayed in some countries, including Tanzania, where presumptive administration of artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) began in July 2007. Case 1 involved a 3-year-old female diagnosed with P. falciparum malaria in May 2007 while in Tanzania. She was treated with a quinine-based regimen and clinically recovered. During her pre-departure medical examination, she received presumptive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. After arriving in the United States on June 12, 2007, she developed fever, chills, and cough on June 25, 2007, and was admitted to a local children’s hospital on June 27, 2007. A blood smear revealed 7% hyperparasitemia with P. falciparum. She was treated with oral atovaquone-proguanil, clinically improved, and was discharged after five days of hospitalization. Case 2 involved a 9-year-old female who arrived in the United States on July 23, 2007. Before leaving Tanzania, she received a 3-day presumptive treatment course of artemether-lumefantrine, with the last dose administered on July 19, 2007. She became ill on August 11, 2007, with fever, headache, malaise, and cough. She was evaluated in a local emergency department on August 14, 2007, where blood smear and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing confirmed P. ovale infection. She was treated with atovaquone-proguanil and later received primaquine to prevent relapse. The CDC recommends presumptive treatment for P. falciparum malaria in U.S.-bound refugees at high risk of infection to prevent severe complications or death after arrival. To be effective, the treatment regimen must be completed no sooner than three days before departure. This approach reduces malaria-related morbidity and mortality among refugees, who often face barriers to accessing healthcare and may experience delays in diagnosis and treatment. However, healthcare providers in the United States may not always be familiar with recommended malaria treatment regimens, as evidenced by the inadequate treatment provided to the patient in Case 1, who received oral atovaquone-proguanil instead of the recommended intravenous quinidine or artesunate for severe P. falciparum infection. Presumptive pre-departure treatment for malaria in geographically clustered refugee populations, such as those in camps, is logistically simpler and more cost-effective than treating symptomatic cases dispersed across the United States. It also reduces the risk of reintroducing malaria into the United States, where the Anopheles mosquito vector is widespread. A recent malaria outbreak in the Caribbean due to reintroduction underscores this risk. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) administers presumptive treatment for P. falciparum malaria to refugees resettling from Tanzania before their departure to the United States. In 2005, the CDC recommended ACT as presumptive treatment for P. falciparum malaria in sub-Saharan African refugees. However, Tanzanian refugees received sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine until July 7, 2007, despite high resistance rates. The artemether-lumefantrine regimen has proven effective in field settings in Africa. Two patients in this report, resettled after July 7, 2007, received complete artemether-lumefantrine treatment before departure but were still diagnosed with P. falciparum malaria after arrival. Possible explanations include incomplete treatment, nonadherence to the medication regimen, poor medication absorption, reinfection, or treatment during a stage of the parasite’s life cycle unaffected by the regimen. In response, the IOM now directly observes all six doses of artemether-lumefantrine treatment and provides milk with each dose to improve absorption. Current IOM policy targets P. falciparum infection only. However, cases of P. ovale malaria in this series involved relapses after arrival in the United States. P. ovale and P. vivax infections are generally less severe than P. falciparum infections but can relapse due to dormant liver-stage hypnozoites. Primaquine is the only agent available to eliminate these parasites, but pre-departure presumptive treatment with primaquine is not recommended due to logistical challenges, cost, and the risk of severe hemolytic anemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)-deficient patients. Healthcare providers caring for refugee populations resettling from malarial regions should remain vigilant for malaria, regardless of prior treatment.
